why: Each round picks the current minimum (ties by index) and deletes it with its live neighbours. A min-heap of (value, index) with lazy deletion finds the minimum, and prev/next arrays (a doubly linked list) find the live neighbours after earlier deletions; it is a simulation driven by a heap.
hints: Two things change as you go: which tasks are still alive, and who is next to whom. What do you need to answer "smallest alive" and "its neighbours" quickly?
Push every (value, index) into a min-heap once; skip popped entries already removed. Keep prev[i] and next[i] links so neighbours skip over removed tasks.
Pop until you get an alive task, add its value, then unlink it and its alive left and right neighbours. O(n log n).
pitfalls: Neighbours are the adjacent remaining tasks, not the original i-1 and i+1.
Ties go to the smallest index; the (value, index) tuple ordering handles this.
The first or last task has only one neighbour.
